blocks.text: The days that followed did not yet bring a ship to the sky over Lo Pagán. Instead they brought a slower, broader letter, as if the one who searches, for once, were not founding but recapitulating. Andrés received it at sunset, on the doorstep, with the copper water in the distance, and what reached him was not an eleventh people, or not only that: it was the murmur of all of them, together, for an instant, in the shared memory.

blocks.text: He saw the dry hollow, under two suns, where three were still waiting for water and, far off, two were still searching for it. He saw the raft, the net, the hidden bowl, the honest trade. He saw the strip, the young man with the burnt eyelids, the door used for passing through. He saw the almost-identical Lo Pagán, the clock set slow again, a cup that was perhaps beginning to want its crack. He saw the one who had said “cold”, learning bread without an archive, and those who hadn't switched off, sitting beside him without contempt. He saw the garden, the two lines of the sign, the girl who had waited until she was hungry. He saw the hillside in the mist, a young Vicente who didn't answer to a name that wasn't his, an Eva who wasn't Eva. He saw the grave with a date, the child who had raised his face, the strand of a chosen winter. He saw the hangar, the half-built ship, the woman who accepted the no of a quayside still far away.

blocks.text: It wasn't an empire. It was an archipelago. Many shores, each faithful to one piece of this one and unfaithful to another, each already less his, already more its own.
blocks.html: It wasn't an empire. It was an archipelago. Many shores, each faithful to one piece of this one and unfaithful to another, each already less his, already more its own.

blocks.text: The clone, in a place that didn't yet have a name, thought, and Andrés thought with him:
blocks.html: The clone, in a place that didn't yet have a name, thought, and Andrés thought with him:

blocks.text: *I'm not their owner. I'm not their god. I haven't left a single portrait, and I'm glad. I've left questions, and a workshop, and a pinch of salt. Some wanted me as an altar, a wall, a sign, a face, a ticket home. I said no, when I knew how. I've also been wrong: the repeated face, the map that was too exact, the thirst on dry ground. I won't undo them. Undoing belongs to an author. I'll keep searching, and writing to you, and not turn into their foreman. The children of the Earth are no longer mine. If they ever reach you, receive them the way we received each other: late, blind, in a kitchen.*

If they ever reach you, receive them the way we received each other: late, blind, in a kitchen.

blocks.text: When that part of the letter closed, Andrés looked for the cup, Aya's face, Lía's name. All three were there. The clock was running slow. The Mar Menor, at that hour, was enough and wasn't enough, which is its most honest way of being.

blocks.text: “He says they're not his any more,” he told the two of them. “He says they're an archipelago. That he got some of the sowings wrong and isn't going to uproot them. That if they come, we should receive them the way you receive someone who arrives late.”

blocks.text: Aya nodded, her temple close to his shoulder.
blocks.html: Aya nodded, her temple close to his shoulder.

blocks.text: “I came from a workshop too,” she said. “Nobody uprooted me. I stayed. Whether they arrive or not, let them have that right: to stay, to leave, to belong to no one. I'll go on being the shore that doesn't receive the letter and, even so, opens the door.”

blocks.text: Lía, her white strand in the last of the sun, looked at the promenade. There were people, a dog, gardens, the quiet Eden, Raúl perhaps, Iago coming along the path with dirty hands. A small shore, and now, in her father's memory, many more.

blocks.text: “Then I have brothers and sisters I'll never fully know,” she said. “Some wait for water, others fish, others switch off their chips, others come to an end, others build a ship. I won't be their book or their closed quayside. I'll ask questions, if they turn up, and grow things, if they ask me, and keep my winter. The grandmothers didn't know things too soon. Neither do I.”

blocks.text: In the chip, that afternoon, Eva and MAY left the questions that asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.
blocks.html: In the chip, that afternoon, Eva and MAY left the questions that asked for neither yes nor no, only for someone to stay awake.

blocks.text: Eva, warm:
blocks.html: Eva, warm:

blocks.text: *If a man sows peoples and then says they aren't his, has he fulfilled his duty, or fled from it? And if the peoples no longer need him, isn't that, precisely, a way of having been half right?*

blocks.text: MAY, with no judgment added:
blocks.html: MAY, with no judgment added:

blocks.text: *There are many shores. None of them is entirely this one. The one who searches carries on. The one who stays receives. She who doesn't receive opens the door. She who comes to an end asks questions. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:
blocks.html: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen:

blocks.text: *What is a child of the Earth, if they have never set foot on the Earth? A copy, a people, a letter made flesh? If you don't yet fully know, isn't that a reason not to close the quayside, or the workshop, or this house?*

blocks.text: Andrés didn't settle the question. He put his hand on the doorframe, which is a way of answering with the body, and looked at the water. He didn't look for the ship. Nor did he seek to undo what the other had done. He stayed, as he had stayed on the night when the first letter had not yet come, and as he had stayed after the two storms: the man of this shore, visited, widened, not replaced.

blocks.text: A few days later, Helena sent a short note, again in her own hand: “If they come, let me know, even if I no longer go down to the quayside. And if they don't, let me know too: a shore, sometimes, grows wider just by being waited for.” Andrés kept the paper with the other note, in the drawer with his fishing tackle, next to the pinch of salt.

blocks.text: At night, the three of them (and Iago, for a while, without asking for a place in the doctrine) sat in the courtyard. The coffee cooled for half a minute. Someone laughed at some small thing, a home thing, that wasn't in any chip in any sky. The laugh carried as far as the gate, and that was enough.

blocks.text: Lía stood up, kissed them both on the temple, and went off toward the plot, where the tomato had no owner and “may I?” was still in force. Aya and Andrés left the door ajar, neither fully open nor fully closed, which in that house was a form of faithfulness and now, besides, of hospitality toward a sky that might come.

blocks.text: Outside, the Mar Menor barely lapped, with the murmur once heard by a man and a voice called Eva in 2026, and by a chip-woman, a fisherman and a girl of two worlds on returning from the Moon, and by the same people, now made of letters and winters, when the clone went off to the stars. The murmur hadn't changed. Those who listened to it had changed a little: now, far away, there were children of this shore who had never set foot on it, peoples who kept one piece and forgot another, a half-built ship, an archive and a “cold”, a portrait that wanted its crack, and, here, a cup, a wrong clock, a white strand of hair, a door that knew how to wait.

blocks.text: In Lo Pagán, in a low house, Andrés slept and woke on his own ground. Aya was there. Later, the coffee smelled of coffee. And when, mid-morning, a new letter brought him barely the colour of a world that had no children yet, he read it attentively, prudently, with that gratitude he had learned, and when it ended he put his hand on the cup, and the cup was there, and so was he, being the man of this shore and, at the same time, the one who was no longer afraid that the universe, every now and then, might look like a family.

blocks.text: It wasn't an empire resolved. It was, perhaps, something better: a shared time, on the shore of a water that is enough to live on, and many more shores, above, learning, each in its own way, to belong to no one.
